source.title: TopK Language Models
source.authors: Ryosuke Takahashi; Tatsuro Inaba; Kentaro Inui; Benjamin Heinzerling

record.tranche_reason: The paper studies sparse activations and neuron specialization in TopK language models, but it does not test the claim versions’ proposed superposition geometry, capacity account, or evidence about ordinary LLM representations. It cites related SAE work but does not test the cited superposition findings.
record.gate_note: The paper reports neuron-entropy, steering, and training-trace results in TopK models. These do not test any listed version: the models are deliberately trained with TopK sparsity, and the study does not measure overlapping feature directions, feature competition for capacity, or SAE recovery of features in ordinary LLMs. Language-model benchmarks and architecture ablations are not included as claim results.
record.test_reason: The paper proposes an architecture (TopK activation inside the LM) and showcases its interpretability. It does not test whether features are superposed in toy or ordinary models, whether capacity drives polysemanticity, or whether SAE features are canonical. It cites SAE shortcomings (seed instability, architecture dependence) only as motivation. The dense baselines have higher neuron entropy, but that is a comparison, not a superposition test. The sparsity is imposed by design.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that TopK LMs keep competitive performance (modest perplexity increase) while neurons become more concept-specialized, single-neuron steering works, and neuron formation can be traced across checkpoints and layers.
record.recipe_differences: The paper trains transformer language models with TopK activation functions in selected layers; it does not reproduce the toy-network setup or measurements of Toy Models of Superposition.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported specialization differs with hidden dimension and layer placement: the wider TopK model has lower entropy, and entropy rises in the final two non-TopK layers. The paper also compares models with different depths in appendix figures and reports the same broad pattern.

fits_no_version.finding: TopK LMs show lower token entropy (about 6–7 vs 9.3–9.5 early) and lower semantic entropy (3.0–3.7 vs 4.3–4.4) than dense baselines. Entropy rises in the final dense layers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Imposing TopK activation sparsity in LM layers yields more token- and semantically-selective neurons than in dense baselines.

fits_no_version.finding: Neuron selectivity sharpens over training, and one dimension (894) becomes 'work'-selective across nearly all layers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In TopK LMs, concept-selective neuron dimensions emerge over training and align across residual-stream layers.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding offsets to single low-entropy neurons steers generations toward the assigned concept (qualitative, one prompt).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Single-neuron interventions in TopK LMs steer generation toward associated concepts.

record.problems: The interpretability showcase is based on small-scale models (the paper reports experiments primarily on models around 1B parameters), and the steering examples are qualitative, use a single prompt, and rely on manually assigned concept labels. The entropy figures show standard deviations, but the text does not provide exact per-layer values for the plotted curves. The paper does not test superposition geometry or compare its neuron units with SAE features.
record.rows_left_out: Language-model benchmark and architecture-ablation results were omitted because they do not measure a claim-version subject. Appendix entropy figures for 8- and 16-layer models are described as showing the same general pattern; they were not added as separate rows because the text gives no separate numeric values.

untested.parts: No toy-model geometry, sparsity-dependent phase transition, or feature directions are measured.
No test of features competing for capacity. Width affects entropy (wider is lower), but that is not a test of dedicated versus shared dimensions.
No test of polysemanticity arising without capacity pressure.
Dense-baseline neuron entropy is reported only as a comparison. No SAE is trained, and features spread across neurons in ordinary LLMs are not measured.
SAE instability is cited, not tested. No SAE features are compared with TopK neurons.
No test of 1-D versus multi-dimensional features.

record.verdict_notes: The Table 2 caption mentions neuron 21:1957 ('energy'), which does not appear in the table; this is a minor internal inconsistency. The steering rows (r8–r11) induce the effect by intervention and are qualitative. The entropy rows have a dense baseline but measure selectivity under imposed sparsity, not superposition.

versions.untested_parts: No toy-model superposition geometry, sparsity-dependent transition, or regular feature geometry is tested.
No test of feature competition for capacity, or of important features receiving dedicated dimensions while others share.
No test of whether polysemanticity arises without capacity pressure.
The study does not test whether ordinary LLMs distribute features across neurons or whether an SAE recovers such features. Its models are trained with an explicit TopK activation constraint.
No test of whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units.
Tracking one neuron index across layers and checkpoints does not test whether features superposed in a network are 1-D directions rather than multidimensional.

rows.subject: TopK LM (D=1024, L=24)
rows.operation_detail: Compared layer-wise token entropy with the dense baseline.
rows.baseline: Dense baseline: approximately 9.3–9.5 in early layers, dropping in middle layers and rising to around 8–9 near output layers.
rows.value: TopK model: approximately 6–7 across layers, with an increase in the final two non-TopK layers.
rows.uncertainty: One standard deviation is shown as shaded regions; exact values not stated.
rows.note: The paper reports the TopK pattern across the two dimensions; the exact D=1024 curve values are not separately stated.

rows.subject: TopK LM (D=2048, L=24)
rows.operation_detail: Compared layer-wise token entropy with the dense baseline.
rows.baseline: Dense baseline: approximately 9.3–9.5 in early layers, dropping in middle layers and rising to around 8–9 near output layers.
rows.value: TopK models are reported at approximately 6–7 across layers; the D=2048 variant has lower entropy than the D=1024 variant. Entropy rises in the final two non-TopK layers.
rows.uncertainty: One standard deviation is shown as shaded regions; exact values not stated.
rows.note: The paper describes the TopK values jointly and notes the relative ordering of the two dimensions.

rows.subject: TopK LM (D=1024, L=24)
rows.operation_detail: Compared layer-wise semantic entropy with the dense baseline.
rows.value: TopK variants: approximately 3.0–3.7, with a rise in the final two non-TopK layers.
rows.uncertainty: Standard deviations are shown; exact values not stated.
rows.note: The paper reports the TopK range across variants, not an exact D=1024 value.

rows.subject: TopK LM (D=2048, L=24)
rows.operation_detail: Compared layer-wise semantic entropy with the dense baseline.
rows.value: TopK variants: approximately 3.0–3.7; the D=2048 variant has the lowest values among the TopK variants, with a rise in the final two non-TopK layers.
rows.uncertainty: Standard deviations are shown; exact values not stated.
rows.note: The paper reports the TopK range across variants, not an exact D=2048 value.

rows.subject: 24-layer TopK LM
rows.size_stated: 24 layers; hidden dimension not stated for this result
rows.operation_detail: Tracked token entropy across training checkpoints in the last TopK layer and final non-TopK layer.
rows.measure: Average token entropy and its lower range across checkpoints
rows.value: The lower range of token entropy in TopK layers decreases as training progresses.
rows.note: No numeric checkpoint values are given in the text.

rows.subject: 24-layer TopK LM

rows.operation_detail: Tracked semantic entropy across training checkpoints in the last TopK layer and final non-TopK layer.
rows.measure: Average semantic entropy and its lower range across checkpoints
rows.value: The lower range of semantic entropy in TopK layers decreases as training progresses.
rows.note: No numeric checkpoint values are given in the text.

rows.subject: 24-layer TopK LM
rows.size_stated: 24 layers; hidden dimension not stated for this result
rows.operation_detail: Tracked the response of hidden dimension 894 to token “work” across layers and checkpoints.
rows.value: Up to 10³ steps the selective response is confined to lower layers; later the same dimension shows strong selective activation across nearly all layers.
rows.note: The authors present this as an example of progressive neuron specialization.

rows.subject: TopK LM
rows.operation_detail: Added a constant offset to neuron 22:894 at every sequence position to steer generation.

conditions.value: δ in [5, 30] produced the most pronounced effects
temperature 0.7; top-p 0.9; top-k 50; up to 128 tokens

rows.baseline: Unamplified completion begins with a story about two brothers.
rows.value: Amplification produced work-related text about a power plant, projects, engines, and driving, with some repetitive or incoherent content.
rows.note: The paper reports qualitative steering, not a rate or magnitude of an uninduced behavior.
